Great article -- still have some sections to read, but it's just too much to read. Emotionally, that is.

Part of me feels the pang of regret and shame seeing so many little details I researched and dreamed[1] (ha!) of prototyping ~2.5y ago expressed and validated so cleanly. Obviously A) I never did get the prototype working nor publish the underlying ideas and B) this blog post (paper? ...plog post?) is building on it at a scale and with quality I could never dream of (fig. 3 is especially striking), not to mention all the new ideas mixed in. Still... sharing cause it helps, I think, and because I expect y'all can relate; if you're old enough, it's very similar to the feeling you get when you think about how much Apple stock you could've bought in the 90s.

Anyway, more materially:

1. Pretty interesting to see Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Opus 5 tied on the basic memory test (aforementioned fig. 3); the Opus comparison alone seems to imply either a hard plateau or that 5.5's huge improvements were accomplished by making good practices more likely, but the Sonnet detail throws that for a loop... I suppose the plateau explanation isn't contradicted, so maybe that's right (for this benchmark).

2. Fig. 4 is gonna do rounds on Reddit and Twitter, my god. Pretty stellar, intuitive depiction of the Mythos step-change that enabled true agentic engineering for the first time this summer! The highlighting is also just the right amount of facetious; love it.

3. Pretty bummed to see no followup philosophy references. We know you have them, Anthropic nerds! Do not be ashamed of the soft and slippery.

4. I am now reminded that I knew they were trying dreaming at scale, as I'm actually on the waitlist for it! And that backs up my overall takeway, actually: I can't help but feel like they're either A) vastly underestimating the amount of CogSci literature that could help them go beyond the "dreaming is when you think in your offtime" paradigm, or B) not sharing their real learnings.

Today's RSI announcement and the final sentence of this seminal plog post being a pitch for enterprise customers supports the latter, I think. That's ostensibly a good thing from a societal stability perspective, but I can't help but feel left out -- not to mention paralyzed by fear of the known unknown...

Reading such a passionate take as someone who has looked up is a strange experience, I must admit. Kinda like how the Bernard twist in S01 of Westworld felt. I'll try to respond as substantively as I can, regardless:

  That Claude rarely, if ever, actually "remembers". Since these are just random markdown files randomly injected into the tiny context.
Complaining about your anecdotal experiences with Claude(Code, hopefully?) isn't a serious criticism, the markdown files are optimized to not be random, and calling 1,000,000 tokens of context "tiny" seems like a plainly unreasonable bar. How much of War and Peace can you hold in your head at once and quote flawlessly, and is it more than 133%?

  What a useless experiment
The experiment is testing their fixes to the problem you lamented just one sentence prior.

  Define "effectively"
They do exactly that in figure 3, as mentioned at the end of the sentence you're quoting. Opus 5 used that advice to raise its benchmark score by 46.8%, and Opus 4.7 used it for a gain of 82.7%. The specific benchmark looks far from trivial, too: https://github.com/pgasawa/continual-learning-bench/tree/mai...

  Then it's not "memory". It's just telling the model to read a text/spec file before implementing something
It fits the colloquial definition, and there is no specific scientific definition in CogSci, CogPsych, Neuro, CogNeuro, NeuroPsych, nor philosophy. There's lots of useful ones offered in different contexts, but they differ considerably.[1] Regardless, it's well accepted industry jargon at this point: it doesn't matter in the same way that it doesn't matter than databases can never truly be "queried" because they can't engage in linguistic discourse.

  So, random injection of random things into context that depend on whether the short ToC entries have any relevance on what Claude is doing
Isn't this inevitably, undeniably true of any possible memory system, just from, say, a big-O perspective? If you have to persist every item in a list to decide which one is relevant enough to load into the same pool of memory, there's no point in the second step anymore.

  What is this bloated article about?
This article is very plausibly wrong, misguided, or even philosophically bankrupt, but I don't see any support for the claim that its topic is unclear. It's discussing the efficacy of proactive state management during idle periods for longrunning LLM-backed agents.

E.g.:

- The memories were hidden away and clearly not written for human eyes; useful for low-stakes ledgers, frustrating when the right kind of errant note can derail a longrun 2 weeks later.

yfontana · Nov 7, 2026

For most dev work I ask claude code / codex to plan larger work as epics and stories (after ideation / brainstorm if needed). I find that this works well to let the AI, my coworkers and me track what has been done so far and what's left in the backlog. Sometimes I direct it on how to split the work, sometimes I don't.

When analyzing my session logs, I tried to look at how story size relates to how much work the AI had to do to fully implement it (made easier by my sessions always having epic#.story# - like 2.6 - in their name). Neither "story size" nor "AI work" have fully obvious metrics, so I looked at a variety of things, like length of story plan, number of lines of codes written for the story, number of different files read/written (and for AI work: number of tool calls, number of tokens for main thread / implementer / reviewer subagents, etc.).

The pattern is always pretty much the same: smaller stories are less token-efficient. One major factor for this is that in bigger stories, the average number of lines of code written per tool call is significantly higher (and not just a little bit, if I remember correctly it's a factor of 1 to 3 between my smallest and largest stories).

None of this is scientifically rigorous, but it's consistent over a fairly significant sample (about 60 stories up to this point). I'm also only measuring amount of work and not quality, but when I find things wrong with a story, I generally ask the AI to fix the issues in the same session, so the two should be correlated (sometimes the issues are large enough that they require new, separate stories to fix, but this is normally caused by problems in ideation and/or planning, not implementation). This is enough to encourages me to ask for more rather than less per story. It might also not apply to everyone, I'm sure this is dependent on everyone's workflow and way to work with the AI. But yeah, that's the sort of stuff you can explore when analyzing your session logs.
